Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Robert Swan's life reads like a boy's own adventure tale with a modern eco-twist. Robert Swan was the first man to walk to both the North and South Poles. Inspired by the daring age of Antarctic exploration, Swan followed in the footsteps of his heroes; the men who risked, and lost, their lives to reach the South Pole. At the age of 29 he embarked on an expedition to the South Pole that was unsupported -- a trek that required him to pull his own sleigh and that lacked medical support crews. By the time he was 33 he had become the first man to walk to both the North and South poles unsupported. But for Swan, the epic journeys to the Poles, and the sailing and overland adventures that have followed, unearthed more than just a spirit for adventure. He experienced firsthand the impact of humanity on the environment when under the hole in the ozone layer at the South Pole, the harsh ultraviolet rays from the sun burned his skin and permanently changed the color of his eyes. It firmed a desire to preserve the fragile natural world and to educate and inspire others, particularly the next generation of decision-makers to do the same. "As the last unspoiled wilderness on Earth, Antarctica is currently protected by the treaty prohibiting drilling and mining until 2041. Decisions made by today's youth will impact our entire planet's ecosystem and the future of life on earth," he says on 2041.com. His polar icewalks gained international attention and in 1992 he was asked to speak at the UN Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, later gaining an OBE and being appointed Special Envoy to the Director General of UNESCO in recognition of his work. At the Earth Summit in Rio he committed to a "global mission" to remove 1,500 tons of waste from Antarctica. Swan and a team of young people from across the world were successful in cleaning up the Russian Antarctic base of Bellinghausen by 2000, making it inhabitable for wildlife again. Foresight, planning and determination then are not alien to a man who spent five years sourcing the funding for his first Antarctic expedition, and Swan's latest project is taking an even longer-term view. Swan founded his organization "2041" in 2003 in order to further his mission of action and education. Named after the year in which Antarctica's protection against mineral exploitation ends, Swan regularly takes business people, teachers and students on expeditions to Antarctica to impress on those with the capacity to enact change that preservation of the environment is essential and achievable. Continuing the green mission on the continent by minimizing the human footprint in the region, his international teams have helped design and build the world's first education station in Antarctica that is run solely on renewable energy. Add to the expeditions, ocean voyages on a boat with sails made from recycled plastic bottles, and it's clear that the veteran polar explorer is a man who is doing all he can to protect and preserve the Antarctic.

# The Last Explorer: Robert Swan's Race to Save the Ice

**A CNN-Style Profile**

---

*By staff correspondent*

**ANTARCTICA** — The wind here doesn't just blow; it interrogates. It finds every seam in a parka, every gap in resolve. Robert Swan has felt that wind for more than three decades, and he says it's changed — subtly, but unmistakably — since he first walked to the South Pole in 1985.

"The ice doesn't lie," Swan says, his voice carrying the flat, weathered cadence of a man who has spent a career being frozen, sunburned, and occasionally terrified in the name of a larger point. "You can argue with a politician. You cannot argue with a melting glacier."

Swan, 68, is not a scientist. He is, by his own description, "a professional explorer" — one of a vanishing breed who made his name doing what seemed, at the time, faintly absurd: walking to both poles unsupported, becoming the first person in history to do so. But somewhere along the way, the walk stopped being the point.

## From Adventure to Alarm

In 1985, Swan led a three-man team on a grueling 900-mile trek to the South Pole, arriving half-blind from UV damage and having lost most of his team's supplies to circumstance and miscalculation. It was a feat of raw endurance, the kind of story that made front pages and barroom legends.

But it was what he saw *after* the walk that redirected his life. Returning to Antarctica years later, Swan noticed the ozone hole overhead had grown. Ice shelves he remembered as solid had begun to fracture and calve at rates that alarmed even the scientists he consulted.

"I went down there as an explorer chasing a horizon," he says. "I came back an environmentalist, whether I wanted the job or not."

## Building "2041"

That transformation led Swan to found the 2041 Foundation, named for the year the Antarctic Treaty — the international agreement banning mining and military activity on the continent — comes up for review. Swan has made it his mission to ensure that when that year arrives, there's enough global will to keep Antarctica protected.

To that end, he's spent the last two decades hauling something arguably more difficult than sledges across the ice: people. Business leaders, students, and young scientists from dozens of countries have joined his expeditions, part of a deliberate strategy to create witnesses — people who've stood on the ice and can't unsee what they saw.

"You can show someone a graph," Swan says. "Or you can put them on a boat, sail them past a glacier, and watch their face when a piece of it the size of a cathedral falls into the sea. One of those things changes people. It's not the graph."

## A Complicated Legacy

Critics have questioned whether flying hundreds of people to the bottom of the world to teach them about climate change is itself an act of environmental contradiction. Swan doesn't dodge the criticism; he's heard it for years.

"Every trip we run, we work to offset, and yes, it's imperfect," he says. "But show me a perfect environmentalist and I'll show you someone who's never left their house. I'd rather bring people face to face with the problem than protect my own purity."

It's a pragmatism that has defined Swan's second act: less interested in ideological cleanliness than in results, alliances, and the slow, unglamorous work of changing minds one delegation at a time.

## The Long Walk Ahead

These days, Swan splits his time between expeditions and the lecture circuit, telling boardrooms and classrooms alike about a continent most of them will never see firsthand. He talks about renewable energy with the same intensity he once reserved for surviving the trek to the Pole — as though it's simply the next brutal, necessary expedition.

His son, Barney Swan, has taken up an active role in the foundation, a passing of the torch that Swan treats with equal parts pride and urgency. There isn't time, he suggests, for the mission to rest on one generation.

Standing on the deck of an expedition ship, with the ice fields stretching toward a horizon he's walked toward more than once, Swan reflects on what's actually being protected.

"People think I'm trying to save Antarctica," he says. "I'm not. Antarctica will be fine, in whatever form it ends up in. What I'm trying to save is us — whether we're smart enough to leave one place on Earth alone."

The wind picks up. Somewhere beyond the ship, ice that has existed for thousands of years continues its slow, quiet argument with time.

---

*This profile is a fictionalized illustrative piece styled after CNN feature journalism.*

# The Long Walk Home: Robert Swan's Journey from Polar Explorer to Planet's Advocate

In 1986, Robert Swan stood at the South Pole, having just completed a grueling 900-mile trek across Antarctica on foot—the first person in history to walk to both poles. He expected to feel triumphant. Instead, he felt something closer to alarm.

"I looked up and the sky was a strange color," Swan has recalled in numerous talks since. "I later learned I'd witnessed, without knowing it, the effects of the ozone hole." That moment of unwitting scientific observation marked a turning point—not just in Swan's life, but in how the world would come to think about polar exploration itself.

## From Conquest to Conservation

Swan's path to the poles was the stuff of classic adventure narrative. Inspired by the ill-fated Antarctic expeditions of Robert Falcon Scott, he organized the "In the Footsteps of Scott" expedition, walking unsupported to the South Pole in 1985-86. Four years later, he led the "Icewalk" expedition to the North Pole, completing an unprecedented feat: traversing both of Earth's poles on foot.

But where earlier generations of polar explorers were driven largely by nationalism, scientific curiosity, or personal glory, Swan emerged from the ice with a different mission. The pristine, brutal landscapes he'd crossed were changing—and not gradually. Sea ice patterns were shifting. The ozone layer above Antarctica was thinning. The very environment that had nearly killed him during his expeditions was itself under threat.

## Founding 2041

In 1992, Swan founded the 2041 Foundation, named for the year the Madrid Protocol—the international agreement banning mining and mineral exploitation in Antarctica—comes up for review. The choice of name was deliberate and urgent: Swan understood that the protections weren't permanent, and that public awareness would be essential to renewing them.

Through 2041, Swan has spent decades bringing people directly to Antarctica—students, business leaders, policymakers—to witness the continent's fragility firsthand. His reasoning is straightforward: abstract warnings about climate change rarely move people the way direct experience does. Standing on ice that scientists say is disappearing tends to concentrate the mind.

The organization has also pushed renewable energy demonstration projects, including establishing a research station powered entirely by renewable energy in Antarctica—proving, quite literally on the coldest continent on Earth, that fossil-free power is viable.

## The Explorer's Argument

What makes Swan's advocacy distinctive is his framing of environmentalism not as sacrifice but as its own form of exploration and challenge. He often argues that climate change represents the "greatest expedition" of this generation—requiring the same discipline, courage, and collective effort that historic polar journeys demanded.

This reframing has proven persuasive to audiences who might otherwise resist environmental messaging. Swan doesn't preach guilt; he issues expedition-style challenges. Sustainability, in his telling, isn't about deprivation—it's about the kind of hard, purposeful work that explorers understand instinctively.

Now in his sixties, Swan has passed some of the literal walking to his son, Barney Swan, with whom he's undertaken subsequent polar expeditions focused explicitly on renewable energy demonstrations—including a South Pole expedition powered entirely by renewable energy sources, without fossil fuels.

The elder Swan's transformation—from a man seeking to conquer geography to one advocating for its protection—mirrors a broader shift in how society thinks about wilderness and human achievement. The poles, once symbols of what humans could conquer through willpower and endurance, have become, in Swan's telling, symbols of what humans stand to lose.

In the frozen silence of Antarctica, where the horizon stretches unbroken and the cold strips away every pretense, Robert Swan found his life's purpose—not despite the danger, but because of it.

## Walking Where Few Had Walked

Born in England in 1956, Swan grew up captivated by stories of the great polar explorers—Shackleton, Scott, Amundsen. Their tales of endurance against impossible odds didn't just entertain him; they ignited something that would define his entire life. While others admired these legends from a comfortable distance, Swan became obsessed with a singular, audacious goal: to retrace their footsteps and become the first person in history to walk to both the North and South Poles.

Three years later, he completed the polar double by reaching the North Pole, cementing his place among history's great explorers.

## The Moment Everything Changed

But it was during these expeditions that Swan witnessed something that would redirect the entire trajectory of his life. Standing in landscapes that seemed eternal and untouchable, he began noticing changes that shouldn't have been there. Increased UV radiation burned his skin and damaged his eyes in ways previous explorers hadn't documented. The ozone hole above Antarctica wasn't an abstract scientific concern—it was a physical reality searing his face.

More profoundly, Swan realized that Antarctica, this seemingly indestructible fortress of ice, was not immune to humanity's impact. The very extremity that made it awe-inspiring also made it a sensitive barometer for environmental change. He watched pristine environments show signs of contamination and stress. The continent that had tested his physical limits was now revealing something more urgent: it was fragile, and it was warning us.

Swan realized that raw survival and personal glory, the currency of traditional exploration, meant nothing if there was no world left to explore. The poles weren't just conquered—they needed to be protected.

## From Explorer to Advocate

This revelation transformed Swan from an adventurer seeking personal achievement into an environmental messenger. He understood that his unique credibility—as someone who had physically endured what few humans ever would—gave him a platform to speak about environmental protection with authority that armchair activists could never claim.

He began to see Antarctica not merely as a destination, but as a symbol: the last truly wild continent on Earth, governed by an international treaty that banned military activity and mineral exploitation, preserved through unprecedented global cooperation. It represented what humanity could achieve when nations set aside self-interest for a greater purpose. But this protection wasn't permanent—the Antarctic Treaty's mining ban was set to be reviewed in 2041.

That date became Swan's new North Star.

## Building 2041: A Movement Born from Ice

Swan founded the 2041 Foundation with a clear and urgent mission: to preserve Antarctica by ensuring the mining ban would be extended indefinitely when it came up for review, and more broadly, to use Antarctica as a living classroom for teaching the world about sustainability and renewable energy.

He didn't simply lecture from podiums—he brought people directly into the environment that had transformed him. Through expeditions like the International Antarctic Expedition, Swan invited students, business leaders, and future policymakers from around the world to stand where he had stood, to feel the same overwhelming vastness and fragility that had rewired his understanding of humanity's relationship with nature.

His philosophy became refreshingly practical: rather than only warning people about environmental destruction, he demonstrated solutions. He established Antarctic research stations powered entirely by renewable energy, proving that even in Earth's harshest environment, sustainable technology could thrive. If clean energy could work at the bottom of the world, his message implied, it could work anywhere.

## The Explorer's Legacy Redefined

Robert Swan's transformation—from a man chasing personal records to a global advocate for planetary preservation—offers a profound lesson about how personal experience can catalyze purpose. He didn't set out to become an environmentalist; the ice itself educated him, burning lessons into his skin and consciousness that no lecture hall could have taught.

His story reminds us that true exploration isn't just about reaching new places—it's about what we do with what those places teach us. Swan walked to both poles seeking to test human limits. He found, instead, the limits of the planet itself, and dedicated the rest of his life to ensuring those limits would be respected.

Through 2041, Swan continues to insist that the fate of Antarctica—and by extension, the fate of our planet—remains undecided, waiting to be shaped by the choices of generations who have yet to stand on that ice, yet who can still choose to protect it before it's too late.
